bullets: Scrooge: ‘Hard and sharp as flint’, ‘solitary as an oyster’.
Stave 5: ‘as light as a feather… as happy as an angel… as merry as a school-boy… as giddy as a drunken man’.
The fog ‘came pouring in at every chink and keyhole’.
The church tower’s bell ‘peeping slyly down at Scrooge’.
Shop goods in Stave 3: onions ‘winking’, pears and apples clustered in ‘blooming pyramids’: the food seems alive with joy.
‘The cold within him froze his old features’.
Stave 3 shop windows overflowing with food: abundance.
Stave 4 Old Joe’s shop: ‘rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal’: squalor.
Lists create **excess**: of greed, of plenty, or of decay.
Hyperbole creates humour and emphasises feeling.

callouts.p: Name the device → quote the precise words → explain the image → say the effect on the reader → link to the theme or Dickens’s purpose.

exam.q: Explore how Dickens uses language to present Scrooge in this extract (Stave 1). (20 marks)
exam.tip: Part (a) rewards precise analysis of 4–6 language choices.

mistakes.r: Say what the simile suggests and why it matters.
mistakes.w: ‘Dickens uses a simile to describe him.’

quotes.a: Scrooge is hard and unyielding; flint sparks fire but never has.
Food personified as joyful and abundant.

quotes.q: rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal
as giddy as a drunken man

summary: Dickens’s descriptive style relies on similes, personification, lists and hyperbole to make people, food and places vivid, comic or frightening; learn the best examples and how to analyse them for part (a).

terms.d: A comparison using like or as.
